solutions.text: The passage explicitly retires the ignorance theory and replaces it with a developmental mismatch: the reward-processing limbic system matures before the self-controlling prefrontal cortex, the gap is widest in mid-adolescence, and peers amplify the pull of reward. The claim that teenagers cannot grasp danger at all is the very view the passage overturns, and it states the opposite order of maturation to the reversed version. Permanent brain damage and denial that the phenomenon exists appear nowhere.

Looms larger is figurative: the expected gain carries more psychological weight than the expected loss, so for the adolescent the reward is felt to matter more than the harm. Nothing in the passage concerns physical size, duration in memory or measurement precision; peers only intensify the effect.

The researchers claim solar radiation management could cool the planet quickly and cheaply while buying time for emission cuts, so it would act on temperature faster than cuts alone. The critics say the opposite of removing greenhouse gases (the cause is left untouched), their worry is about stopping abruptly rather than an inability to stop, and no consensus on immediate deployment is claimed.

A sedative dulls a symptom without curing the disease: here the symptom is temperature and the cause is greenhouse gases, so the metaphor says the technique relieves a symptom of warming without removing its cause. Medically dangerous, illegal, unmodelled and overpriced readings import ideas the passage never raises.

Travel is figurative: accuracy measured on data resembling the training set may not hold in ordinary clinics with different cameras, lighting and patients, so it may fail to transfer to settings unlike those it was trained in. The confidentiality, price, literal-journey and refutation readings are absent from the text.

The thesis sits in the final sentence: a clinic needs a deployment study, performance measured where the machine will actually be used, rather than a headline benchmark on training-like data. The passage endorses the technology, so its rejection or the redundancy of specialists overstates it; training exclusively in ordinary clinics distorts the proposal, and scanner costs never appear.

Follow the chain: starved of fibre, some microbes eat the gut mucus instead, and that mucus is the barrier shielding the body's own tissues, so chronic fibre deficiency may weaken the barrier protecting gut tissues. The fatty acids come from microbes, not human enzymes, and the hedged wording supports no absolute claims about all microbes or exclusive causes.

Roughage is the everyday name for dietary fibre, the indigestible plant material human enzymes cannot break down, exactly as the passage's opening clause defines it. Meat proteins, refined sugars, vitamins and the mucus lining do not fit the in-passage definition.
Italy's Constitutional Court has fifteen judges, each serving a single non-renewable nine-year term. The number nine belongs to the US Supreme Court and is the classic confusion here.

Article 135 splits the appointments into equal thirds: five judges named by the President of the Republic, five elected by Parliament in joint session and five by the supreme ordinary and administrative courts. Any single-body formula breaks the deliberate balance, and there is no popular election.

The sequence is fixed: referendum and Constituent Assembly on 2 June 1946, approval on 22 December 1947, entry into force on 1 January 1948. The April 1948 and 1949 dates fall after it, and the 1946 and 1947 dates earlier in the same chain.

The constitutional text runs to 139 articles, organised into fundamental principles, Part I on rights and duties and Part II on the organisation of the Republic, plus transitional provisions. None of the smaller figures matches the official count of articles.

The electoral college is both chambers in joint session plus three delegates per region (one only for Valle d'Aosta, fifty-eight in all); two thirds is required for the first three ballots, an absolute majority thereafter. The election is indirect, so direct popular voting describes other republics, not Italy.

Italy has perfect bicameralism: the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate of the Republic sit for five years and hold identical powers, voting on the same bills. The Council of State is an administrative court, and regional councils or municipal representatives are not parliamentary chambers.

Under Article 94 a new government must appear before both chambers and obtain their confidence within ten days of appointment; either house can withdraw it by a reasoned motion. Confidence is not a presidential, senatorial-only or judicial prerogative.

Constitutional law 1 of 2020 cut Parliament to 400 deputies and 200 elected senators, first applied in 2022, nearly halving the previous 630 and 315. Any pair containing 630 or 315 belongs to the pre-reform chambers.

The Court's primary function is judging the constitutionality of national and regional laws. It also settles conflicts between organs of the state and between state and regions, and tries the President for crimes against the Constitution, but it never hears ordinary criminal appeals or private disputes.

Article 1 reads: Italy is a democratic Republic founded on labour, with sovereignty belonging to the people who exercise it in the forms and limits of the Constitution. The monarchy fell in the 1946 referendum, and neither confederal, presidential nor property-based wording appears.
Five regions hold special statutes and enlarged autonomy: Sicily, Sardinia, Valle d'Aosta, Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol and Friuli-Venezia Giulia. The remaining fifteen are ordinary-statute regions.

An abrogative referendum succeeds when a majority of valid ballots favour repeal and turnout reaches at least half of those entitled to vote. It is called by 500,000 voters or five regional councils, and taxes, the budget, amnesties and ratified treaties are exempt; no presidential authorisation, prior Chamber vote or seventy-five per cent rule exists.

The President of the Republic appoints the prime minister and, on the premier's proposal, the ministers, and the government must then win the confidence of Parliament in both chambers. Italy elects no prime minister directly, and neither the Constitutional Court, automatic seniority nor the European Council is involved.

Sergio Mattarella took office in 2015 and was re-elected in January 2022 for a second term running to 2029. Napolitano (2006 to 2015) was his predecessor, and Ciampi, Pertini and Cossiga sit earlier in the presidential list.

Giorgia Meloni leads the government formed in October 2022 after winning the September elections, Italy's first woman prime minister, having succeeded technocrat Mario Draghi. Gentiloni, Renzi and Letta are earlier premiers or party figures, not the incumbent.

Festa della Repubblica recalls 2 June 1946, the institutional referendum in which Italians chose a Republic over the monarchy and elected the Constituent Assembly, the first national ballot open to women. Liberation Day falls on 25 April, unification on 17 March 1861, and the Constitution entered into force on 1 January 1948.

The European Central Bank is seated in Frankfurt am Main, where it steers euro-area monetary policy. Brussels hosts the Commission's main offices and Luxembourg the Court of Justice and Court of Auditors; The Hague holds no major EU institution.

The twelve monthly plenary sessions of the European Parliament take place in Strasbourg, its official seat; Brussels hosts committee meetings and the political groups, Luxembourg the General Secretariat. Geneva is not an EU seat at all.

The Court of Justice of the European Union sits in Luxembourg. The deliberate trap is the European Court of Human Rights, which sits in Strasbourg but belongs to the Council of Europe, an organisation outside the EU.

The Commission is the Union's executive: it holds the near-monopoly on proposing legislation, polices compliance as guardian of the treaties, and consists of one commissioner per member state under its president. It is neither a court, a parliament, a speakers' assembly nor a committee of central-bank governors.

The European Council unites the heads of state or government of the member states with its own president and the Commission president, setting the EU's general political direction from Brussels. The foreign ministers form the separate Council of the EU, which legislates alongside Parliament, a frequent confusion.

The Treaty of Rome of 25 March 1957 established the European Economic Community among six founders (Italy, France, West Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg). Coal and Steel came from Paris 1951, NATO from Washington 1949, and the EU itself from Maastricht 1992.

Signed in 1992, Maastricht transformed the communities into the European Union and fixed the convergence criteria opening the path to the single currency. The EEC already existed (1957), the Council of Europe is older still and not an EU body, and Schengen is the 1985 agreement applied from 1995.
Notes and coins entered circulation on 1 January 2002 in twelve countries; the euro had existed since 1 January 1999 only as book money. The 1999 date is the standard trap.
After the UK's withdrawal on 31 January 2020 the Union counts 27 member states, the first and only reduction in its history. Croatia, the 28th entrant of 2013, remains the most recent to join.
Croatia joined on 1 July 2013 as the 28th member, the most recent accession to date. Bulgaria and Romania came in 2007, Slovenia and Hungary in 2004.

On 1 January 2023 Croatia achieved a double first: it became the twentieth euro-area member and simultaneously joined the Schengen area, retiring its old kuna. Withdrawing from the Union or Schengen, or adopting the kuna or the Swiss franc, inverts the facts.

Bulgaria's former currency was the lev, converted at the fixed rate of 1.95583 lev per euro when it became the twenty-first euro country on 1 January 2026. The dinar belongs to Serbia, the koruna to Czechia, the zloty to Poland and the forint to Hungary.

Schengen is the zone in which participating countries have abolished controls at their common internal borders; it overlaps with, but is not, the EU (Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein take part, while EU members Ireland and Cyprus do not). It is not a military alliance, a currency union or an agricultural scheme.

The European Union received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012 for over six decades of advancing peace, reconciliation, democracy and human rights in Europe. None of the other years listed carries this award.

The European Parliament is the only EU institution elected directly by citizens, every five years by universal suffrage since 1979; the June 2024 election seated 720 MEPs. The Commission, the two Councils and the Courts are all appointed bodies.
Denmark keeps its krone under a negotiated opt-out from the euro (the krone is nevertheless pegged through ERM II). France, Spain, Portugal and Greece are all euro users from the currency's start.

The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861 in Turin, with Vittorio Emanuele II as first king. Veneto arrived in 1866 and Rome in 1870, so those later dates mark enlargements, not the proclamation.

Giuseppe Garibaldi led the Thousand, landing at Marsala in 1860, conquering Sicily and Naples and handing the south to Vittorio Emanuele II. Cavour directed diplomacy from the north, Mazzini inspired from exile, and Gioberti was a pamphleteer, none of them commanding the expedition.

Camillo Benso di Cavour, Piedmont's prime minister, secured Napoleon III's support at Plombières (1858), fought Austria in 1859 and engineered the plebiscites of 1860 that attached central Italy. Einaudi was a later Republic's president, Crispi a later premier.

Mazzini founded Giovine Italia (Young Italy) in 1831 and gave the Risorgimento its republican, unitary ideal, the soul of the triad completed by Cavour's statecraft and Garibaldi's sword. He was no king, viceroy, scientist or fascist ideologue.

Troops breached Porta Pia on 20 September 1870, ending papal temporal rule, and Rome formally became the capital in 1871, after Turin (1861 to 1865) and Florence (1865 to 1871). The 1870 date marks the capture, 1871 the transfer of the capital.

In May 1915 Italy entered the war on the Triple Entente side (France, Britain, Russia), despite its 1882 Triple Alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary, after the secret Treaty of London promised Austro-Hungarian lands. Neutrality had covered 1914 only, not the whole war.

Caporetto, in October 1917, was the German-Austrian breakthrough that shattered the Italian front and forced the retreat to the Piave, avenged a year later by victory at Vittorio Veneto. Custoza and Lissa were the defeats of 1866, Marengo a Napoleonic battle of 1800, El Alamein a 1942 desert battle.

The March on Rome of October 1922 ended when Vittorio Emanuele III declined to sign the state of siege and appointed Mussolini prime minister, so power passed through a constitutional door. No king abdicated, the Republic came in 1946, and the Lateran Pacts are 1929.

The 1929 Lateran Pacts (a political treaty, a concordat and a financial convention) created the sovereign Vatican City State and settled the Roman Question open since 1870. They did not touch Venice, the League of Nations or Trentino-Alto Adige, nor did they nationalise Church property.

On 25 April 1945 the National Liberation Committee called a general insurrection as the German retreat began, and Milan and Turin freed themselves; the date is kept as Liberation Day. The institutional referendum belongs to 2 June 1946, and the other events are unrelated to the date.

The vote of 2 June 1946 chose a Republic over the monarchy (about 54 to 46 per cent) and elected the Constituent Assembly, the first national election in which women voted. The first President, De Nicola, was chosen by Parliament, not directly, and NATO dates from 1949.

The economic miracle ran from the late 1950s into the early 1960s (peak roughly 1958 to 1963): booming industry and exports, the Fiat 500 and mass migration from south to north. The Fascist 1930s, the reconstruction years and the 2000s all miss it.

The Red Brigades kidnapped Aldo Moro on 16 March 1978 and murdered him on 9 May 1978 after 55 days in captivity, the climax of the Years of Lead. Piazza Fontana (1969) and Bologna station (1980) bracket but do not date the Moro case.

Growing out of a Milan bribery inquiry in 1992, Clean Hands exposed Tangentopoli, the systemic bribery that financed the governing parties, and swept away Christian Democracy and the Socialists, ending the First Republic. War criminals, banks, the constitution's labour articles and football doping were not its targets.

Leonardo painted the Last Supper (about 1495 to 1498) on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, experimenting with tempera on dry wall, which explains its famous flaking. The Louvre keeps his Mona Lisa, not this mural.

The David (1501 to 1504) has stood in the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence since 1873; a replica marks its original spot outside the Palazzo Vecchio. The Uffizi is Botticelli's home ground, not the David's.

Michelangelo carved the Roman Pietà around his twenty-fourth year and signed it, his only signed work; it rests in St Peter's Basilica behind glass installed after the 1972 hammer attack. Florence's Accademia houses the David, a different masterpiece.

The School of Athens (1509 to 1511), painted for Pope Julius II, adorns the Stanza della Segnatura of the Vatican Apostolic Palace, with Plato and Aristotle at the centre. The Sistine Chapel is Michelangelo's domain, the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua Giotto's.
Botticelli's Birth of Venus (about 1485) hangs in the Uffizi in Florence beside his Primavera, twin icons of Medici-era Neo-Platonism. The London, Paris and Rome collections named hold other works.
The Sistine ceiling with its nine Genesis scenes was painted between 1508 and 1512; the altar-wall Last Judgement came a quarter-century later, 1536 to 1541. The two date-pairs must not be swapped.

Brunelleschi raised the double-shell dome of Florence Cathedral, completed by 1436 without traditional wooden centring and still the largest masonry dome, and he also codified linear perspective. St Paul's dome in London is Wren's, and the Leaning Tower is Pisa's Romanesque bell tower.

The present Pantheon was rebuilt under Hadrian around 126 AD; only Agrippa's name survives on the façade from the 27 BC original, hence its inscription. Augustus, Trajan and Nero belong to other phases, and Constantine's building came later.

Begun under Vespasian around 70 to 72 AD, the Flavian Amphitheatre was inaugurated by Titus in 80 AD with a hundred days of games. Dates BC predate the Empire, and 315 AD suits the nearby Arch of Constantine era instead.

Caravaggio's revolution is tenebrism: violent contrasts of light and dark with unsparing realism, saints with dirty feet, as in the Calling of Saint Matthew in Rome's San Luigi dei Francesi. Cubism and impressionism postdate him, neoclassicism opposes his idiom, and gold-ground flatness is medieval.

Bernini shaped Baroque Rome: the colonnade embracing St Peter's Square (1656 to 1667) and the Ecstasy of Saint Teresa (1645 to 1652) in Santa Maria della Vittoria. The Florence dome is Brunelleschi's, the Accademia David Michelangelo's, and the Padua frescoes Giotto's.

Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD and buried Pompeii under ash and pumice, sealing the Roman city until excavation; Pliny the Younger's letters describe the catastrophe. Earthquakes and wartime bombing damaged the site but never produced its preservation.

The Comedy counts 100 cantos in three canticles (Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso), composed around 1308 to 1320 in terza rima in the Tuscan vernacular, the choice that made Dante the father of the Italian language. Writing in Latin would contradict its founding act, and the Council of Trent came two centuries later.

Boccaccio's frame: ten young Florentines shelter from the 1348 plague in a villa and tell ten stories each over ten days, one hundred novelle in all. The dream-tour of the afterlife is Dante's poem, and single narrators or exchanged letters fit neither the Decameron's structure.

Petrarch is the father of Humanism: his rediscovery of classical texts and the inward, self-scrutinising lyric of the Canzoniere (addressed to Laura, the perfected sonnet) opened the Renaissance; he was crowned poet laureate in Rome in 1341.

Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513, the founding text of political realism, counselling that a ruler is safer being feared than loved. The Courtier is Castiglione's book, Utopia is More's, and Erasmus wrote satire rather than statecraft.

The Betrothed (definitive edition 1840) unfolds in seventeenth-century Lombardy under Spanish rule: Renzo and Lucia, war, bread riots and the plague of Milan of 1630, which Manzoni also dissected in The Column of Infamy. It is a historical novel set two centuries before its writing.

Umberto Eco, the Bologna semiotician, wrote The Name of the Rose (1980), the fourteenth-century monastery murder mystery whose detective friar William of Baskerville nods to Sherlock Holmes (filmed with Sean Connery). Levi, Calvino, Morante and Deledda wrote other kinds of fiction.

Luigi Pirandello took the 1934 Nobel in Literature for his theatre of the unstable self, of which Six Characters in Search of an Author is the emblem. Italy's other literature Nobels are Deledda 1926, Quasimodo 1959, Montale 1975 and Fo 1997.

Primo Levi, a Jewish chemist from Turin deported to Auschwitz-Monowitz, wrote If This Is a Man, the survivor's testament whose prefacing poem begs the reader to consider whether this is a man; The Truce followed it.

Invisible Cities (1972) is Italo Calvino's catalogue of fifty-five impossible cities that Marco Polo describes to Kublai Khan, each in the end a reflection of Venice. Lampedusa's classic is The Leopard, and Eco wrote the medieval whodunit instead.

The Neapolitan Novels, from My Brilliant Friend onward, tracing Lila and Lenù from 1950s Naples, are published under the pseudonym Elena Ferrante, whose real identity has never been confirmed. Fallaci, Ginzburg, Tamaro and Maraini are named, identifiable writers.

The allegory of the cave occupies Book VII of Plato's Republic: prisoners take shadows for reality until one climbs toward the sun, Plato's image of education as ascent to the Forms. The Symposium treats love, the Phaedo the soul, and the Nicomachean Ethics is Aristotle's work.

Publishing the Dialogue in 1632 cost Galileo trial before the Roman Inquisition and condemnation in 1633, with abjuration and house arrest, during which he wrote the Discourses on Two New Sciences. Jupiter's moons had been discovered back in 1610, and the Church's rehabilitation came only in 1992.

The sentence opens Rousseau's Social Contract of 1762, whose standard of legitimacy, the general will, electrified the French Revolution and modern democratic theory. Hobbes opens from the war of all against all, a different first move and a different politics.

Gabriel García Márquez published One Hundred Years of Solitude in 1967, the century-spanning saga of the Buendía family in Macondo and the emblem of magical realism; he took the Nobel in 1982. Borges wrote compressed fictions, Vargas Llosa and Cortázar other kinds of novels, and Allende published later.

Marconi shared the 1909 Physics Nobel with Karl Ferdinand Braun for wireless telegraphy, the technological root of radio. The electric battery is Volta's (1800), the telephone Bell's, the transistor Bell Labs' in 1947, and fission was detected in 1938.

Volta built the voltaic pile in 1800, the first electric battery, coaxing steady current from stacked copper and zinc discs; the volt honours his name and Napoleon honoured the man. Neptune, X-rays and the periodic table belong to other scientists, and the transatlantic radio signal is Marconi's feat.

Chicago Pile-1, under Fermi's direction, went critical on 2 December 1942 beneath the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. The Via Panisperna institute in Rome was his earlier laboratory, Los Alamos and Oak Ridge later Manhattan Project sites, and CERN is a peacetime laboratory.
CERN straddles the Franco-Swiss border near Geneva. Founded in 1954, it detected the Higgs boson in 2012 and is where Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989.

Galileo's 1610 observations, announced in Sidereus Nuncius, revealed the four largest moons of Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto), along with lunar mountains and the phases of Venus, evidence that not everything circles the Earth. Neptune awaited 1846, and the Martian canals were a later optical illusion.

Avogadro's law (1811): equal volumes of any gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, whatever their identity or weight; it grounds the mole and Avogadro's number of 6.022 × 10²³. Equal mass fails at once for gases of different molecular weight.

Fleming's 1928 observation of Penicillium mould destroying staphylococci on a neglected plate gave penicillin; Florey and Chain turned it into a drug in time for the D-Day landings, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel. Aspirin, insulin, the polio vaccine and chloroquine have entirely different origins.

Watson and Crick built the double-helix model at Cambridge in 1953, building crucially on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction work (Photo 51) at King's College London; the 1962 Nobel honoured Watson, Crick and Wilkins, Franklin having died in 1958. Pauling had proposed a triple helix, wrongly.

The 2024 Physics Nobel went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks, physics-trained methods behind today's AI. Gravitational waves, the Higgs and the blue LED were recognised in 2017, 2013 and 2014, and superconductivity honours went to other physicists.

The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on 25 December 2021, observes primarily in the infrared, its 6.5-metre gold-coated segmented mirror parked at the Sun-Earth L2 point to catch light from the earliest, red-shifted galaxies. Hubble is the visible-light predecessor; gamma rays, radio and ultraviolet belong to other observatories.

After Pope Francis died on 21 April 2025, the conclave of 8 May 2025 elected Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost: Pope Leo XIV, born in Chicago in 1955, an Augustinian long active in Peru and the first pope from the United States. Parolin, Zuppi, Tagle and Erdő were widely named contenders, not the choice.

The 2026 Winter Olympics ran 6 to 22 February 2026 at Milan and Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy's third Winter Games after Cortina 1956 and Turin 2006. Turin alone dates to 2006, and the Scandinavian and Austrian cities listed host no 2026 Games.

Spain won the first 48-team World Cup by beating Argentina 1–0 after extra time in the final of 19 July 2026 at MetLife Stadium, Ferran Torres scoring in the 106th minute for a second Spanish title after 2010. Argentina's bid for back-to-back crowns failed at the last step, and France, Portugal, Brazil and England fell short of the trophy.

Paris 2024 was that city's third Games (after 1900 and 1924); the Summer Olympics next go to Los Angeles in 2028, and then Brisbane in 2032. The other city-year pairings do not exist on the calendar, and the Summer Games keep their even-year, four-year rhythm.

The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize went to María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader, for her fight for democratic rights; her daughter collected the medal in Oslo while Machado stayed in hiding. Nihon Hidankyo, the Japanese atomic-bomb survivors' group, was the 2024 laureate, and the WHO, the IAEA and Zelensky have not won it.

The 2024 Nobel in Literature went to Han Kang, the first South Korean laureate, author of The Vegetarian and Human Acts. Ishiguro won in 2017, Ernaux in 2022, Fosse in 2023, and Hungary's László Krasznahorkai followed as the 2025 laureate.

Donald Trump, winner of the November 2024 election, was inaugurated on 20 January 2025 as the 47th president, joining Grover Cleveland as the only presidents to serve two non-consecutive terms (he is both the 45th and the 47th). Biden and Harris were the outgoing ticket, and a third Obama term is constitutionally barred.

The 2025 ordinary Jubilee, on the usual twenty-five-year rhythm and under the motto Pilgrims of Hope, was centred on Rome, opened by Francis at St Peter's on 24 December 2024 and closed by Leo XIV on 6 January 2026. Lourdes, Assisi, Jerusalem and Mexico City host no universal Holy Year of 2025.

Clarke, Devoret and Martinis won the 2025 Physics Nobel for the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit, the physics that superconducting qubits inherit and hence the foundation of superconducting quantum computers. Fusion reactors, mRNA vaccines, perovskite panels and satellite navigation are unrelated fields.

The 2025 Medicine Nobel honoured Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries on peripheral immune tolerance: regulatory T cells and the FOXP3 gene, the immune system's brakes, knowledge central to autoimmunity and transplant medicine. MicroRNA took the 2024 prize, mRNA vaccines 2023, CRISPR the 2020 Chemistry prize and hepatitis C the 2020 Medicine prize.
